details:
**The Course of Empire**
Cole's five-painting series (1833–1836) depicting the rise and fall of an imaginary civilization in the same valley, commissioned by New York merchant Luman Reed. The paintings are The Savage State (hunters in a wilderness), The Arcadian or Pastoral State, The Consummation of Empire, Destruction, and Desolation. A distinctive rocky crag topped by a boulder appears in the background of every painting to identify the setting.

**The Oxbow**
Cole's most famous painting (1836), formally View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm. The left side shows dark storm clouds over untamed wilderness and shattered trees, while the right side shows sunlit cultivated farmland along the dramatic oxbow-shaped bend of the Connecticut River, contrasting wilderness and civilization.

**Hudson River School**
The mid-19th-century movement of American Romantic landscape painters, named for the Hudson River Valley of New York, of which Cole is considered the founder. Other members included Asher Durand, Frederic Edwin Church (Cole's student), and Albert Bierstadt.

**Destruction**
The fourth painting of The Course of Empire, showing invaders sacking the classical city amid a storm. A bridge collapses under a fleeing crowd, and a headless statue posed like the ancient Borghese Gladiator lunges forward holding a chipped shield; Cole's signature appears on its pedestal.

**Desolation**
The final painting of The Course of Empire, showing the moonlit ruins of the abandoned city reclaimed by nature, with no humans present. A single ivy-covered column, topped by a bird's nest, dominates the foreground.

**"Noah" in Hebrew and the self-portrait in The Oxbow**
Logging scars on the distant hillside of The Oxbow appear to spell "Noah" (נח) in Hebrew letters, which read upside down (as from heaven) resemble "Shaddai," meaning "the Almighty." Cole also included a tiny self-portrait of himself at his easel among the rocks and shrubbery at the bottom of the painting, looking out at the viewer.

**The Voyage of Life**
Cole's four-painting allegorical series (1840, Childhood, Youth, Manhood, Old Age) following a voyager in a boat down the river of life, accompanied by a guardian angel. In Childhood an infant emerges from a cave in a golden boat; in Youth a young man steers toward a castle in the clouds; in Old Age an old man looks toward heaven as light breaks through. The series was popularized by engravings by James Smillie.

**Kindred Spirits**
An 1849 painting by Asher Durand made as a tribute after Cole's death, showing Cole and the poet William Cullen Bryant standing together on a rock ledge overlooking a gorge in the Catskills. It was sold by the New York Public Library to Alice Walton and is now at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art.

**The Titan's Goblet**
An 1833 fantasy painting of a colossal stone goblet standing in a landscape, its rim covered with vegetation and small buildings, while tiny sailboats float on the water inside it.

**The Architect's Dream**
An 1840 painting in which a man (the architect) reclines on a column atop giant books, gazing at an imaginary panorama of architecture from different eras, including an Egyptian pyramid, a Greek temple, and a Gothic cathedral.

**"Essay on American Scenery"**
Cole's 1836 essay praising the American wilderness as a source of the sublime and lamenting its destruction by development. It ends by warning that through "ignorance and folly" we are shutting ourselves out of "the walls of Eden."

**Expulsion from the Garden of Eden**
An 1828 painting in which Adam and Eve leave the radiant Garden of Eden through a rocky gate into a dark, hostile world, with a volcano erupting in the background.

**The Departure and The Return**
A pair of 1837 paintings depicting a medieval lord and his knights riding out from a castle in the morning light, then returning wounded and defeated at sunset.

**L'Allegro and Il Penseroso**
A pair of 1845 paintings inspired by John Milton's companion poems, contrasting a cheerful pastoral landscape with a melancholy, contemplative one near Lake Nemi in Italy, in which a woman kneels before an outdoor shrine of the Virgin and Child.

**Scene from The Last of the Mohicans**
Cole painted several scenes from James Fenimore Cooper's novel, including one showing a circular gathering of figures on top of a mountain plateau surrounded by vast wilderness. He also painted Daniel Boone sitting at the door of his cabin with a staff and a dog.
